Find papers that appear more than once in a Scholar export

Source: R/duplicates.R
find_duplicate_papers.Rd

Google Scholar sometimes lists the same paper twice: a journal version and a preprint, a re-indexed copy with one citation, or a reprint with a new year. In a co-authorship network that makes two authors look as if they wrote more papers together than they did. This function flags likely duplicates without changing your data.

Usage

find_duplicate_papers(
  data,
  title = "title",
  authors = "authors",
  year = "year",
  cites = "cited_by",
  sep = "\\s+and\\s+",
  method = c("near", "exact"),
  max_dist = 0.08,
  require_author_overlap = TRUE
)

Arguments

data

A data frame of papers, such as the result of [scholar_parse_html()] or [bib_to_df()].

title, authors, year, cites

Names of the columns holding the title, the author string, the year, and the citation count. If there is no `authors` column but there is an `author` column (as from [bib_to_df()]), that one is used. Missing year or citation columns are allowed.

sep

Regular expression separating authors in the author string. Default `"\s+and\s+"`.

method

`"near"` (default) or `"exact"`.

max_dist

For `"near"`: the largest edit distance, as a share of the longer title. Default 0.08 (about 1 character in 12).

require_author_overlap

Only flag pairs that share an author surname. Default `TRUE`.

Value

A data frame of class `citelens_duplicates` with one row per flagged paper: `group`, `row` (row number in `data`), `title`, `year`, `cited_by`, `authors`, and `keep` (`TRUE` for the most-cited row in each group). It has zero rows if nothing is flagged.

Details

Two rows are treated as the same paper when their titles match after lower-casing, folding accents, and removing punctuation and extra spaces (`method = "exact"`), or when they are within `max_dist` of each other by edit distance (`method = "near"`, the default, which also catches a missing word or a typo). By default a pair is flagged only when the rows also share at least one author surname, so two different papers that happen to have a generic title are not merged.

The `"near"` method compares every pair of titles, so memory and time grow with the square of the number of rows. It is fine for a few thousand references; for much larger files use `method = "exact"`.

See also

[dedupe_papers()] to remove the copies, [find_duplicates()] to find near-duplicate entries by abstract similarity instead of by title.

Examples

f <- system.file("extdata", "sample_authors.csv", package = "citelens")
papers <- read.csv(f, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
dups <- find_duplicate_papers(papers)
dups   # review before removing anything
#> 1 group(s) of likely duplicates; 1 row(s) would be dropped.
#> 
#> Group 1
#>   KEEP row 1    2018 | Alder, A. and Birch, B. | 120 cites | Persistence gaps in first-year cohorts
#>   drop row 7    2019 | Alder, A. and Birch, B. | 1 cites | Persistence gaps in first-year cohorts.
#>
